assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation) moved timekeeping to the 1e-18 level and has become a precision probe of relativity, gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale and possible variation of constants. It is a clean, controllable quantum experiment where every physical detail matters, which is the kind of result I value; the discovery is the concept and its realization, not an application.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea (2001-2003) and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye's group drove it to record accuracy and stability, with many JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE contributions. A two-person prize looks defensible; other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Hollberg) could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and surpassed across many laboratories, with international comparisons and a pending redefinition of the SI second. Recognition is timely and the physics is stable.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as an incremental extension of earlier frequency-metrology prizes (Ramsey, Hall and Haensch) or as a distinct discovery.
Priority between the lattice proposal and the many experimental refinements; I am relying on memory of the history and have not verified it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits and underpins nearly all superconducting quantum processors; dispersive readout and the transmon-resonator architecture are decisive. It is foundational and has a clear experimental demonstration of a new regime of coupling.
assessment.attribution: Blais (theory, 2004), Wallraff and Schoelkopf (first strong-coupling experiment, 2004) form a natural trio. Yale colleagues (Devoret, Girvin, Huang) and the transmon inventors (Koch et al.) complicate the allocation. I work in this field and am close to several of these groups, so I flag a possible conflict and would defer on attribution to colleagues.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed across many laboratories for two decades. Timing is a question: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and the committee may wish to let some time pass.
uncertainties: Overlap in subject with the 2025 prize and the possible appearance of recognising the same community twice.
Dispersion of credit across Yale, ETH, Sherbrooke and Chalmers-adjacent work.
My own proximity to the field; I do not claim independent verification of priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal made ion-trap quantum computation a concrete physical scheme, and the subsequent experimental gates, entanglement of many ions and quantum simulation established a leading platform. It is important and of lasting impact, though the experimental control of single ions was already recognised in 2012.
assessment.attribution: Theory (Cirac, Zoller) and experiment (Blatt, with Wineland already a laureate and others such as Monroe) is a sensible split. Credit overlaps with B033 and B012 for Cirac and Zoller, so the committee should not recognise the same pair twice for adjacent ideas.
assessment.maturity: Strong, multi-laboratory confirmation, with logical-qubit demonstrations ongoing. Mature as a basic result; the computing application itself is still ahead.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the other Cirac-Zoller candidates.
Whether Monroe or Wineland-group contributions require a different configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the HgTe observation, opened a new class of quantum matter with protected edge states. Its originality and impact are very high and it is a clear case of a theory-experiment pair.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang predicted HgTe and Molenkamp's group observed it. Hasan, Moore and others on 3D topological insulators make a clean allocation delicate. This candidate omits Bernevig and Zhang, so the supplied trio is plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in multiple materials and by independent groups (ARPES, transport); mature and stable. Timely.
uncertainties: Competing credit for the 3D case and for BHZ prediction.
Topological phases were recognised in 2016, so some committee members may see overlap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity in a highly tunable system, creating the moire-materials field. The discovery opened a new regime and is widely influential.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated states and superconductivity (2018). Cory Dean's group, Yacoby, and others contributed, so the trio is plausible but the allocation of experimental credit is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated states is not settled. Slightly early, and I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on how settled the interpretation is.
uncertainties: Open questions about the pairing mechanism.
Sample-to-sample variability reported in early work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Geometric phases (Aharonov-Bohm, Berry's phase) are conceptually fundamental and underlie topological band theory, polarization and holonomic gates, and also appear in superconducting-qubit control. The importance and clarity are very high.
assessment.attribution: Berry's 1984 phase and the Aharonov-Bohm effect are distinct contributions separated by decades; Aharonov-Anandan, Pancharatnam, Simon and Wilczek-Zee complicate the story. The two-name configuration is reasonable but the credit is broad.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed experimentally in many settings for decades; the interpretation is stable. Recognition is long overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Prior-art credit (Pancharatnam, Aharonov-Anandan) and the possible need to include more people.
Whether the committee views it as a unified discovery or a family of results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide controllable quantum simulators of Hubbard models, with the Mott-insulator transition, single-site imaging and many-body dynamics. They bring clean quantum phenomena into a controllable setting.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch-Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization, Greiner-Bloch observed the superfluid-Mott transition, and Bloch and Greiner developed quantum-gas microscopes. Hänsch, Esslinger, Kasevich and Cirac make configuration contested; the supplied list supports at most three.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across laboratories; the question is how much of the simulation promise is realized, since quantitative advantage over classical methods is not yet established.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and 2012 prize.
Fair credit for Esslinger, Hänsch and Cirac.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion (ground-state cooling, strong coupling, entanglement and quantum states of macroscopic oscillators) pushes quantum mechanics to macroscopic objects. It is closely related to my own interests in artificial atoms coupled to phonons, and a clear test of quantum physics at a new scale.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (quantum ground state in a mechanical resonator, 2010), Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg (cavity optomechanics) are all major contributors; Teufel, Lehnert and Painter also made decisive ground-state and strong-coupling experiments, so allocation is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature in cavity optomechanics, with multiple independent confirmations. The scope for applications is still early, so recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 macroscopic-quantum prize in terms of the theme.
Credit for Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and Regal.
